- Jackie Thai asked about the expansion rate of initial commitments, with Bill Ryan citing examples of significant increases in spending within months.

Discussion Summary: Below response provides an objective comparison of Microsoft Copilot, ChatGPT Enterprise, Anthropic Claude, and Google Gemini Enterprise, focusing on security, compliance, and enterprise suitability. Microsoft Copilot is best suited for organizations already invested in Microsoft, offering mature security and regulatory compliance, though it has limited advanced reasoning and vendor lock-in concerns. ChatGPT Enterprise excels in reasoning and flexibility but requires manual governance and carries data transfer risks. Claude is strong in extensibility and security integrations but lacks real-time enforcement and needs extra controls. Gemini Enterprise provides advanced governance and data residency but introduces operational complexity and risk of agent sprawl. Gartner recommends leveraging bundled AI for adoption, avoiding vendor lock-in, and prioritizing built-in security and governance, with detailed gap analysis and supporting resources provided.

•	Complete the cleanup of legacy AIP labels and finalize default label configurations across all regions.
•	Address technical issues identified in POC pilots, particularly Print to PDF errors, to ensure smooth deployment.

Date: 13-Jul-26
Reference Number: 20193163
Buyer Region: ASIAPAC
Buyer Industry: Services
Buyer Role: CIO or Head of Technology
Purpose: IBISWorld Proposal Review
Question Asked: Type of Purchase: Renewal of existing agreement
Vendor: IBISWorld
Type of Proposal: Services

Client wants advice on:
- Pricing Insights/Benchmarking
- Terms & Conditions Review

Background and expected outcomes: 
Review IBIS World API Terms & Conditions & agreement addendum

Are there are any red flags, or missing information from this agreement you would expect to see.
Is there any feedback Gartner would recommend we pass along to the business sponsor for them to be aware of?
Analyst Name: Jaideep Thyagarajan
Discussion Summary: 1. Critical Restriction on OpenAI and Open-Source Models
The Risk: The amendment explicitly mandates that any use of the data must be in a closed system controlled by RSM and "shall not be used for or within any OpenAI model"
. It also prohibits any open-source AI third-party provider from accessing the data or AI output
.
Recommendation: You must urgently verify FabricAI’s underlying architecture. If your tool relies on OpenAI (even through enterprise environments like Microsoft Azure OpenAI) or unauthorized open-source models, signing this puts RSM in immediate breach. We recommend negotiating an "Enterprise AI carve-out" that explicitly permits the use of ring-fenced, enterprise-grade LLMs (like Azure OpenAI) where data is not used to train the provider's foundational models.
2. Draconian API Rate Limits and Suspension
The Risk: The contract imposes a strict hard limit of ten (10) machine calls to the IBISWorld servers per second
. Crucially, IBISWorld reserves the right to immediately suspend your access if this limit is exceeded
. As you scale to all Australian employees, peak usage could easily trigger an unexpected enterprise-wide outage.
Recommendation: Ensure your internal IT team builds throttling mechanisms into the FabricAI architecture to enforce a cap of 9 calls per second. Contractually, push back on the immediate suspension right and negotiate a "soft cap" that requires IBISWorld to notify you and provide a cure period (e.g., 48 hours) before suspending service.
3. Prohibition on External Distribution of AI Outputs
The Risk: Your base license allows for up to 10% of an IBISWorld report to be used in client-facing documents, provided it is properly cited
. However, the AI Amendment overrides this, stating that the AI Tool is for internal decision-making only and explicitly mandates that "there is no external distribution of IBISWorld Data or report content" generated by the AI Tool
.
Recommendation: If RSM consultants intend to use FabricAI to draft client deliverables, advisory documents, or external benchmarking reports, you must align the AI rules with the base agreement. Propose a clause stating that AI-generated insights may be used in client-facing documents under the same 10% fair-use rules outlined in the Base Agreement.
4. Unrealistic Data Purging Requirements
The Risk: If you ever terminate this subscription, the contract requires RSM to "take reasonable efforts to purge or remove any Data within the AI Tool"
. Due to the nature of machine learning, "unlearning" or purging ingested data from an AI model is often technically impossible.
Recommendation: Amend this clause to reflect technical reality. Propose changing the requirement from purging data "within the AI Tool" to deleting all IBISWorld source files from RSM's vector databases and active storage environments.
5. Asymmetrical Liability and Indemnification
The Risk: IBISWorld caps its total liability for negligence or breach to the total License Fee paid during a 12-month period (prorated at $15,000) and completely disclaims any liability for AI outputs
. Conversely, RSM is required to fully indemnify and defend IBISWorld against "any and all damages arising from any Unauthorized Use of the Data" by your employees
.
Recommendation: Do not accept an open-ended indemnification for employee actions. Negotiate a mutual liability cap for unauthorized use (e.g., 2x or 3x the annual License Fee) to protect RSM from uncapped damages.

Buyer Industry: Banking, Finance and Insurance
Buyer Role: CIO or Head of Technology
Purpose: Follow up: LLM prioritization of Earned vs Owned channels (Dhuven)
Question Asked: The client had an initial call 20131398 however it turned out it's a misalignment - the Analyst could not cover the query. 

As a follow up, please can get one of the authors of "Optimize Your Content for Visibility by ChatGPT, Gemini and Other GenAI Search Tools" to have this discussion with the client?

Original brief: There was a question raised by our General Managers community on what percentage prioritization LLM's reference between earned (external validation) vs owned ( websites content etc). I responded stating that this differs but we can look at proportionally 50/50 between the two. And we need to still do both. Does Gartner have any information on this ?
Analyst Name: Lauren Villeneuve
Discussion Summary: Client was no-show -- sent WR (there was a calendar error and they were sorry they missed the call.) 

Hi Sandeep, sorry we missed each other today — I understand that things come up! I wanted to follow up on your question on the "prioritization of earned versus owned content within LLMs and AI-powered search experiences." My recommendation is that organizations should invest in both earned and owned strategies because visibility in AI-generated answers is ultimately influenced by a combination of brand-controlled content and third-party validation.
 
From a directional standpoint, external industry studies suggest that a large majority of LLM citations and recommendations may be influenced by earned media sources (e.g., industry publications, analyst commentary, peer-review platforms, forums, PR coverage, and other third-party references like Reddit), while owned media provides the core source material that helps AI systems understand a brand's products, expertise, and messaging. AI models generally place greater trust in third-party sources when validating brand claims because they are perceived as more objective. But to note: the exact weighting varies significantly by model, query type, industry, and available content, so I would recommend using this directionally.
 
So overall — I agree with you that the key to success in Answer Engine Optimization (AEO) requires strengthening both your owned content foundation and your earned authority across the broader web. My top strategy recommendations to my clients are: 
 
Assess and Prioritize Your AI Visibility Gaps: Evaluate how platforms such as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Perplexity currently represent your brand. Understanding which topics, products, and use cases produce inaccurate, incomplete, or competitor-dominated responses helps prioritize optimization efforts where they will have the greatest impact.
Ungate High-Value Expertise:  Because AI crawlers function similarly to anonymous visitors, valuable resources hidden behind forms or login walls often cannot be discovered or cited. Consider making strategic thought leadership, case studies, technical documentation, and educational content publicly accessible in machine-readable formats.
Focus on a Small Set of High-Value Topics, Then Scale: Rather than attempting to optimize all content simultaneously, start with a focused set of high-priority customer questions, use cases, and buying scenarios. Establish authority in these areas first, measure results, and then expand the approach across additional products, personas, and industry segments.
Create an AI-First Content Architecture: Organize content around topic clusters and pillar pages rather than standalone content assets. This helps AI systems better understand topical depth, relationships between content, and your overall authority within a subject area.
Restructure Content for Machine Extraction: AI systems favor content that is easy to parse and reuse. Incorporate direct-answer formats, FAQs, structured comparisons, bulleted lists, tables, and appropriate schema markup to improve extractability and citation potential.
Build Authority Across Your Website and the Broader Web: This is particularly important given the role earned media appears to play in AI citation behavior. Strengthen machine discoverability through clear content structures, semantic organization, and schema markup on owned properties while simultaneously building credibility through participation in trusted third-party communities, media outlets, review platforms, and industry conversations.
Build Distributed Consensus Across Third-Party Channels: Since LLMs cross-reference information from multiple sources, it is increasingly important that your brand narrative is consistently represented across LinkedIn, industry publications, review platforms, forums, PR placements, and other trusted external destinations. 	· Effective AI risk management requires a combination of controls: policy, technical enforcement (DLP, EDR, enterprise browsers) and user identity management. No single tool is sufficient; a layered, phased approach is best practice.
	· Establishing and communicating a clear AI usage policy is a critical first step. This sets expectations, prepare you for audits, increase compliance and helps drive a culture of security.
	· A gradual rollout of AI access, starting with users who have a valid business case, allows for better risk management and fine-tuning of controls.
	· Using corporate licenses and accounts provides better authentication, monitoring and control over data exposure compared to personal accounts, which pose risks due to synchronization across unmanaged devices.
Solutions like Palo Alto/Prisma, Zscaler, Netskope and enterprise browsers can provide visibility and enforcement. DSPM tools (e.g., Varonis, Cyera, Concentric) help with data discovery, classification and exposure management.

Email follow-up:
It was a pleasure speaking with your team today about enterprise AI search platforms. The key ask was to explore alternative enterprise search solutions for integrating with Microsoft 365 and iManage Cloud, considering the limitations of the current on-premise search engine and the potential of vendors like Deep Judge. 

There are three common approaches to enterprise search: the platform approach, in-application search, and federated search. In-application search, such as Microsoft 365 Copilot and Ask iManage, are deeply integrated with their business application but may lack customisation capabilities. Federated search, using AI assistants like ChatGPT, brokers queries to other search engines and applications, providing distilled answers. As we discussed, I recommend you consider established vendors of enterprise AI search platforms (see Market Guide for Enterprise AI Search and the latest Market Overview for Enterprise AI Search) ahead of startups like DeepJudge. 

Law firms often use a combination of Microsoft 365 for general documents and iManage for legal documents, with iManage serving as the operational system of record.

Enterprise search experiences are rarely successful strategies for search and instead focussing on in-application search quality for iManage and M365 may be a better investment of time and resources. Both iManage and M365 of AI assistants that are well tuned to the environments in which they work. In addition the iManage M365 connector allows Copilot to ground answers in iManage content.

Azure AI Foundry & Purview
AWS Bedrock & Stack

Autonomous AI Use Cases

European Regulatory Alignment

Developer Experience
Unified development with Visual Studio, Copilot Studio, and Azure DevOps.
Greater flexibility, but more complexity; strong developer tools (Cloud9, CodeWhisperer).
Cost & Licensing
Predictable pricing for integrated services; discounts for enterprise agreements.
Pay-as-you-go, granular pricing; more options for cost optimization but can be complex.

Purpose: AI Cost Modeling
Question Asked: Client is interested in understanding the cost implications of implementing AI in procurement, specifically focusing on intake orchestration. She seeks insights to build a business case for potential funding and wants to know the investment required for AI implementation. 

In client's words: "discuss AI cost modeling specifically for intake orchestration, so we have the numbers needed for our summer funding requests."


Questions are - What are the cost implications of implementing AI in procurement, particularly for intake orchestration? What factors drive these costs, and how can they be benchmarked? What are the potential risks and considerations involved in AI cost modeling for procurement?
Analyst Name: Vanessa Hines
Discussion Summary: Key ask:
To build a defensible funding model for procurement AI investments by understanding cost drivers, expected outcomes, and potential build, buy, or blend approaches that could improve procurement capacity and efficiency without requiring a large-scale transformation effort.

Summary:
- The discussion began with AI cost modeling for procurement orchestration and intake-related processes but quickly expanded into broader procurement efficiency and operating model challenges.
- Vanessa Hines clarified that Gartner does not provide implementation-cost benchmarks or rough-order-of-magnitude pricing for AI or orchestration solutions, but can help clients structure funding models, identify cost drivers, and evaluate future proposals.
- Ana Gonsalves explained that the current procurement technology landscape includes multiple disconnected systems supporting intake, project/value management, sourcing, contract management, and spend analytics, creating inefficiencies and manual coordination.
- Ana shared that a recent RFI involving more than 20 vendors did not identify a solution capable of addressing their desired future-state requirements. Discussion explored whether this reflected market limitations, requirements complexity, or broader operating model challenges.
- Vanessa noted that orchestration platforms are often better suited to workflow coordination than replacing multiple source-to-pay technologies and may not solve deeply specialized sourcing, legal, or risk-management activities.
- Ana identified procurement capacity and efficiency as primary concerns, citing approximately 30% year-over-year growth in demand volume coupled with increasing process complexity.
- Discussion explored whether current challenges stem solely from technology gaps or whether elements of the procurement operating model, governance structure, buying channels, and escalation thresholds may also contribute to capacity constraints.
- Ana expressed concern that a full orchestration initiative would require significant cross-functional alignment across procurement, legal, risk, IT, and other stakeholders, making it a difficult enterprise-wide transformation to pursue in the near term.
- Ana indicated growing interest in exploring targeted AI agents and automation opportunities that could address specific bottlenecks with lower organizational lift than a large orchestration platform investment.
- Vanessa discussed build, buy, and blend considerations, noting that organizations increasingly evaluate how existing platforms, embedded AI capabilities, and internally developed agents can be combined to achieve business outcomes.
- Ana shared that her team is working with IT to assess capabilities available through Copilot, ChatGPT, and other AI technologies while also evaluating governance and access constraints.
- Vanessa introduced a framework for evaluating AI investments across four cost categories: technology costs, implementation costs, organizational costs, and ongoing operating costs.
- Discussion highlighted the importance of accounting for consumption-based pricing, usage growth, integration complexity, and governance costs when evaluating AI investments.
- Vanessa recommended building multiple funding scenarios and tying investments directly to business outcomes such as capacity creation, efficiency gains, cycle-time improvements, and increased procurement impact rather than focusing solely on technology acquisition.

Question Asked: The client has developed a comprehensive AI literacy plan and seeks to validate her approach by understanding how other financial and insurance organizations are investing in and structuring their AI literacy initiatives. She is preparing for an upcoming board presentation and requires a detailed, written summary to inform her recommendations.
Specific Questions:

What specific investments (e.g., tools, platforms, learning pathways) are peer organizations making to build and sustain AI literacy?
What scalable options exist for acquiring and maintaining knowledge bases to support ongoing AI literacy?
Analyst Name: Claire Song
Discussion Summary: Hi Elizabeth,
Thank you for your inquiry on AI literacy program investments and best practices. I am Claire Song, Senior Specialist Analyst at Gartner, and I specialize in advising organizations on the topics of AI literacy and AI governance.
I am pleased to provide a written response to your questions listed above. Additionally, I highly recommend setting up a follow-up inquiry or document review with myself or another analyst to receive tailored feedback on your AI literacy strategy.
Please note: Gartner does not currently have financial services-specific research pertaining to AI literacy; in turn, my response is based on the industry agnostic best practices and case studies we have published.
Oftentimes, we see that learning pathways that combine experiential (on-the-job) learning with formal and social learning yield the best results. I advise clients to follow the 70-20-10 rule in which 70% of their AI literacy program is dedicated to experiential learning, 20% to social learning and 10% to formal learning through classrooms or courses. 

For formal learning, it is important to develop short, well-designed microbursts of learning. These bite-size modules can be consumed anytime, anywhere and be brought to the learner at the moment of need, in turn underpinning continuous agile learning. Some examples of formal programs that provide such microbursts include the Google AI Literacy Program, Anthropic Academy and OpenAI Academy.

Your AI literacy program should also incorporate social learning through communities of practice and centers of excellence that bring people together for knowledge sharing and collective learning. These social learning groups should exist at the persona level, focused on AI skills applied to similar roles, and across departments and the enterprise to stimulate and spread learning. Specifically, I recommend starting by identifying use cases with high business impact and building tailored curricula around the personas that are directly involved (e.g., software developers, marketers, managers, analysts) adapted for their level of AI expertise. Then, follow by aligning content to the tools, workflows, and decisions each group encounters and collaborate with these groups to ensure that the training curricula is continuously aligned to their use cases and needs. This practice will be key to ensuring that your AI literacy program continues to be relevant as AI evolves how your employees approach their daily responsibilities. For an example of how one organization implemented persona-based training, please see Solve AI Literacy Gaps With Dynamic Learning Tracks.

Finally, learners must apply new AI literacy skills from learning on-the-job (also called experiential learning). This phase should be supported by the social learning structures including coaching, mentoring, shadowing, paired application of skills and vendor knowledge transfer. Other methods include “learning by doing” via experiments and sandbox environments, proof of concepts and hackathons. 

Another best practice I hear when speaking to clients is specifically investing in/hiring AI educators and equipping them to deliver at scale. AI champions are valuable but not sufficient; in turn, dedicated educators and structured enablement are needed to deliver effective training at scale. These educators ideally should develop tailored curricula, guided exercises, templates, and study plans that can be delivered scalably across teams, keeping in mind the distinct learning needs of the different personas you have identified across your workforce. 

To ensure your literacy program is sustainable, I recommend you utilize an AI literacy scorecard with a feedback loop. To get started, define and track metrics across three dimensions that capture success: success of the program, the employee, and the business. Date: 1-Jul-26
Reference Number: 20090479
Buyer Region: NORTHAM
Buyer Industry: Government
Buyer Role: Transformation
Purpose: Evaluating Anduril and Palantir Capabilities | Jess Ross
Question Asked: Another client within the NNL account had a joint call with analysts Mark Beyer and Jorge Lopez (Ref# 19514351) to get a better understanding of the capacities and limitations of Anduril and Palantir broadly. That client and the Gartner Client Director provided the analyst recommendations to this client - Jess Ross - and she would like to set up a call with the analysts so that she can hear their insights and ask some of the questions she has on this joint effort for NNL.

See the "Additional Client Details" for the original submission request and scope.
Analyst Name: Mark A. Beyer
Discussion Summary: Palantir's core technology stack is composed of four primary interoperable platforms that work together to ingest, manage, and analyze data and AI:

Foundry is the foundational core platform for data integration, data management, and analytics. It handles data ingestion, manages data within a proprietary internal database, and provides visualization and application delivery. Foundry utilizes continuous data profiling, machine learning over usage logs, and graph analytics to resolve the "dissonance" between how data is theoretically designed (ontology) and how it actually exists (taxonomy).

Gotham functions as a metadata analytics and forensics tool. It penetrates the otherwise opaque metadata within Foundry to analyze system operations, optimize processes, and ingest third-party metadata. Gotham is often utilized to "hunt" for additional work or identify new use cases within a client's data landscape.

AIP (Artificial Intelligence Platform) is not a standalone AI or Large Language Model, but rather an AI orchestration engine. It coordinates external third-party AI models (like OpenAI or SageMaker) by feeding them data resident in Foundry and metadata from Gotham, and then integrates the AI outputs back into the Foundry workflow.

Apollo serves as the infrastructure and cloud enablement layer. It manages the continuous delivery and deployment of Palantir's software across various cloud and on-premises environments.

The Professional Services Model and Forward Deployed Engineers (FDEs). Palantir operates on a "coterminous delivery" model, meaning their contracts bundle platform subscriptions, compute and storage usage, and high-end professional services into a single, often open-ended budget. Palantir's primary market differentiation does not stem from its software—which can often be replicated using a best-of-breed stack—but from its highly skilled consulting staff.

The platform is implemented by Forward Deployed Engineers (FDEs), who are "guru-level" data engineers. These FDEs utilize Foundry and Gotham to perform advanced data forensics, identify anomalies, and custom-build the data integration pipelines needed to make the system function.

However, this delivery model creates significant challenges regarding vendor lock-in and knowledge transfer:

The "Black Box" of Metadata: While Palantir's tools generate initial discovery metadata, this metadata is often disconnected from the final production designs (new code, views, pipelines). The institutional memory of exactly why specific data integration decisions were made remains in the heads of the FDEs, rather than being documented in the system.

Knowledge Transfer Failures: Because FDEs operate at such an elite level, they frequently struggle to translate their processes to a client's intermediate or novice staff. In fact, market observations show that virtually no client has achieved enough self-service capability to completely disengage from Palantir's professional services.

Organic Scope Creep: Palantir's FDEs use Gotham's capabilities to explore disconnected systems during their initial data discovery phase. This provides them with opportunities to "hunt" for additional consulting work, which can lead to rapid, organic cost escalation as they expand their footprint across the enterprise.

Data integration projects are notorious for exceeding their budgets and timelines, with final costs typically running 2.5 to 11 times (250% to 1,200%) over original estimates. This near-universal tendency creates massive fatigue and frustration among C-level executives and board members who are tired of delayed and failed data initiatives.

Analyst Name: Robert Stoneman
Discussion Summary: 1.	How does Gartner view the role of AI as a source of national power, comparable to military, economic, and diplomatic instruments?

For more details on this question, I urge you to look at the following research note: Maverick Insights: Treat AI as a ‘Prescription Only’ Controlled Substance to Prioritize Access and Use. I have extracted some of the relevant information below, though, of relevance to the question at hand.

Control over AI models and the underlying technology stack is certainly emerging as a source of national power, comparable to military, economic, and diplomatic instruments. In some regards, this looks almost analogous to how, in the late 1940s and 1950s, nuclear weapons and the risk of proliferation emerged as major forces shaping global politics.  This in effect cemented 60 years of a world order that in many ways still underpins the global security balance today. 

Today, the U.S., China and Europe are the emerging regional superpowers for AI influence. Those alliances can exert outsized pressure on every country to fall in line with either AI excess or AI limits should they choose to. Current political winds do not lean in the direction of greater limits (outside of the EU, at least, with examples of regulation such as the EU AI Act, which seeks to limit appropriate use cases for AI), but a large-scale tragedy or failure of AI might see this change. 

Recent U.S. Department of War involvements with Anthropic and OpenAI highlight the depth to which government use of AI may be either desirable or undesirable. As governments treat AI as more of a national resource, they trigger opportunities to regulate access to it, if for nothing more than self-interest. 

To explore future scenarios further, I strongly recommend having a look at Government 2035: AI and Digital Sovereignty Reshape the Future. This research concentrates on the two principal driving forces for digital governments in the present and forthcoming decade: the trajectory of AI and the degree of digital sovereignty. AI maturity spans from the initial, fragmented utilization of automation to fully integrated agentic systems operating at scale. The spectrum of digital sovereignty ranges from open, globally integrated technology ecosystems to highly sovereign models that prioritize not just control over data, but also operational and technological sovereignty.

Collectively, these dimensions yield a set of divergent future scenarios that facilitate an examination of how governmental operations may evolve under varying technological and geopolitical conditions. By analyzing differing levels of adoption across both dimensions, four key future states have been delineated:
•	Autonomous digital state, characterized by high AI adoption and a strong, closed sovereignty posture.
•	Measured autonomy, characterized by low AI adoption and a strong, closed sovereignty posture.
•	Global platform reliance, characterized by high AI adoption and an open sovereignty posture.
•	The lean reliance state, characterized by low AI adoption and an open sovereignty posture.
